explanations.answer: The same devotion Paul has for them
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, "But thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same devotion I have for you." (2 Corinthians 8:16) Paul doesn't take credit for it. He thanks God. Titus, Paul's partner and fellow worker, has the very same devotion Paul has.

explanations.answer: A wish to lead their church himself
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd go there, friend, since Titus is the one traveling. But the verse says nothing about Titus wanting to lead the church. It says God put into his heart "…the same devotion I have for you." (2 Corinthians 8:16) That's Paul's own love for the Corinthians, and Titus carries it too.

explanations.answer: A worry about how they'd been giving
explanations.explanation: Nope, no worry in this verse, friend. Paul is thanking God here. What God put in Titus's heart was "…the same devotion I have for you." (2 Corinthians 8:16) That's devotion for the Corinthians, plain and simple.

True, baker! Paul says Titus "…is eagerly coming to you of his own volition." (2 Corinthians 8:17) Titus was glad to hear Paul's appeal, and he's coming eagerly on his own. Nobody had to drag him to the door.

Close, but it's true, baker. Paul says, "For not only did he welcome our appeal, but he is eagerly coming to you of his own volition." (2 Corinthians 8:17) Titus welcomed the appeal, and he is eagerly coming of his own volition too. So the statement holds.

Yes, gospel! Paul says this brother "…is praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel." (2 Corinthians 8:18) The good news is what this man spends his work on. And every church praising him? That's a good name to have.

I get the guess, since temple sounds like church work. But Paul says the brother is praised "…for his work in the gospel." (2 Corinthians 8:18) His work is the good news itself. The temple isn't mentioned anywhere in these verses.

SYNAGOGUE, friend? Straight for the holy building, no hesitation. I love that confidence! But Paul says this brother is praised by all the churches "…for his work in the gospel." (2 Corinthians 8:18) It's not a building. The good news itself is what he works on.

That's the one. Paul says the offering is administered "…to honor the Lord Himself and to show our eagerness to help." (2 Corinthians 8:19) It honors the Lord, and it shows how ready Paul's team is to help. Nothing in the verse says it's for anything else.

Whoa, that's a different direction, friend. Paul says nothing about being paid in this verse. The offering is administered "…to honor the Lord Himself and to show our eagerness to help." (2 Corinthians 8:19) Honoring the Lord and showing eagerness to help, that's what Paul says it's for.

Not here, baker. Paul says nothing about power over the churches. In this very verse, the churches chose this brother to travel with the team, and the offering is "…to honor the Lord Himself and to show our eagerness to help." (2 Corinthians 8:19) That's honoring the Lord and showing eagerness.

explanations.answer: Any criticism of how it's handled
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. Paul says, "We want to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift." (2 Corinthians 8:20) He wants the gift handled so well that nobody has a complaint about it. That's careful work, and I like it.

explanations.answer: Any delay in getting it delivered
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since a gift does need to get where it's going. But Paul never mentions delay in this verse. He says, "We want to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift." (2 Corinthians 8:20) His concern is how it's handled.

explanations.answer: Any churches finding out about it
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Paul isn't hiding anything. Just before this, he says the churches chose a brother to travel with the offering. (2 Corinthians 8:19) What he wants to avoid is "…any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift." (2 Corinthians 8:20)

Not this time, baker. Paul says, "For we are taking great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men." (2 Corinthians 8:21) The words "not only" give it away. People's eyes count too, so the statement is false.

Yes, false! Paul says, "For we are taking great care to do what is right, not only in the eyes of the Lord, but also in the eyes of men." (2 Corinthians 8:21) He cares about the Lord's eyes, and he cares about people's eyes too. Both count, and those two little words "not only" are the clue.

explanations.answer: By his great confidence in the Corinthians
explanations.explanation: That's right. Paul says this brother has proven his earnestness "…many times and in many ways, and now even more so by his great confidence in you." (2 Corinthians 8:22) He has a long record already. Now he shows even more by believing in the Corinthians.

explanations.answer: By paying his own way to Corinth
explanations.explanation: Paying his own way, baker? Look at you, spreadsheet open, balancing the travel budget! Paul never says who covers the trip. He says this brother's earnestness shows "…now even more so by his great confidence in you." (2 Corinthians 8:22) The proof is that he believes in the Corinthians.

explanations.answer: By leaving his home to travel
explanations.explanation: Leaving home to travel does sound earnest, friend. Bags packed, door locked, the whole production! But that's not where Paul points. He says this brother's earnestness shows "…now even more so by his great confidence in you." (2 Corinthians 8:22) The proof is that he believes in the Corinthians.
Messengers, you got it, baker! Paul says, "As for our brothers, they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ." (2 Corinthians 8:23) And what a title: the glory of Christ.

Rulers would be a big title, baker, but Paul doesn't use it. He says, "…they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ." (2 Corinthians 8:23) Messengers is the word he picked. Rulers isn't in the verse.

I can see why you'd guess it, with all that talk about watching how the gift is handled. But Paul says, "…they are messengers of the churches, the glory of Christ." (2 Corinthians 8:23) Messengers, not judges.

Yes, the proof of their love! Paul writes, "In full view of the churches, then, show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our boasting about you." (2 Corinthians 8:24) That's what he asks the Corinthians to show, in full view of the churches. It's the second thing he names besides the reason for the boasting.

Respect for Paul's authority? Friend, Paul is not fishing for a standing ovation here! He asks them to "…show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our boasting about you." (2 Corinthians 8:24) Love is on that list. Authority never shows up.

Courage under trial? Baker, you just made this sound like a movie trailer, deep voice and all! But Paul's ask is smaller and warmer: "…show these men the proof of your love and the reason for our boasting about you." (2 Corinthians 8:24) Courage isn't named. Love is.

True, baker! Paul says, "Now about the service to the saints, there is no need for me to write to you." (2 Corinthians 9:1) He says it because he knows their eagerness to help. The next verse spells that out.
Not quite, it's true. Paul says, "Now about the service to the saints, there is no need for me to write to you." (2 Corinthians 9:1) That's his own sentence. The next verse tells you why he says it.

explanations.answer: He knows how eager they are to help
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Paul says, "For I know your eagerness to help…" (2 Corinthians 9:2) He already knows how ready they are, so there's no need to write about the gift. He trusts them.

Titus is on the way, but the verse doesn't say he already told them anything. Paul's reason is, "For I know your eagerness to help…" (2 Corinthians 9:2) His confidence comes from knowing the Corinthians.

explanations.answer: He covered it all in an earlier letter
explanations.explanation: Sounds reasonable, friend, but Paul doesn't say that. His reason is, "For I know your eagerness to help…" (2 Corinthians 9:2) He isn't pointing back to another letter. He's pointing to what he knows about them.
Stirred, yes! Paul says, "And your zeal has stirred most of them to do likewise." (2 Corinthians 9:2) The Corinthians' eagerness got the Macedonians moving too. Zeal like that is catching.
Warned doesn't fit, baker. Paul isn't saying the Corinthians warned anyone. He says, "…your zeal has stirred most of them to do likewise." (2 Corinthians 9:2) Their zeal got the Macedonians moving.

Confused would be a funny result, friend, but it's not what Paul says. He says, "…your zeal has stirred most of them to do likewise." (2 Corinthians 9:2) The Corinthians' zeal stirred them up to give.

explanations.answer: So his boasting won't prove empty
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says, "But I am sending the brothers in order that our boasting about you in this matter should not prove empty, but that you will be prepared, just as I said." (2 Corinthians 9:3) He's been boasting about the Corinthians. He wants them prepared so that boasting holds up.

explanations.answer: So he can ask for a bigger gift
explanations.explanation: Not what the text says, baker. Paul sends the brothers "…in order that our boasting about you in this matter should not prove empty…" (2 Corinthians 9:3) He never asks for a bigger gift. He wants them prepared like he said.

explanations.answer: So they can check on the teaching
explanations.explanation: Checking on the teaching, friend? Sounds like somebody's holding a clipboard and squinting! But Paul sends the brothers "…in order that our boasting about you in this matter should not prove empty, but that you will be prepared, just as I said." (2 Corinthians 9:3) Nothing here about inspecting teaching. It's about the Corinthians being ready to give.

Not quite, baker. Paul says, "…we—to say nothing of you—would be ashamed of having been so confident." (2 Corinthians 9:4) The word "we" means Paul's team would be ashamed too. So it's false that only the Corinthians would be.

Yes, false! Paul writes, "…we—to say nothing of you—would be ashamed of having been so confident." (2 Corinthians 9:4) His team would feel it too, not just the Corinthians. They had put their confidence on the line.

Yes, baker! Paul wants the brothers to "…make arrangements for the generous gift you had promised. This way, your gift will be prepared generously and not begrudgingly." (2 Corinthians 9:5) The gift was already promised. He wants it prepared the right way, and generously is the word he uses.

explanations.answer: Quietly and not in public view
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd go there, friend, but that's not what the verse says. Paul wants the gift "…prepared generously and not begrudgingly." (2 Corinthians 9:5) Earlier he even asks them to show their love "In full view of the churches…" (2 Corinthians 8:24)

That's a reasonable guess, baker, but Paul doesn't set amounts or shares here. He says the gift will be "…prepared generously and not begrudgingly." (2 Corinthians 9:5) The point is the spirit of the giving.
